reusable_lessons.lesson: Before choosing features for any task built around a label or target flag, screen the manifest for label-encoding fields: a column whose non-null count matches the positive-class count (e.g. fraud_pattern_type populated only where fraud_label=1) or whose name references the label encodes it and must be excluded even when it is a catalogue default. State the exclusion and the manifest evidence in the plan rationale.

Never use member sex, race/ethnicity or age band, or close proxies such as payer_type, to characterise, rank or predict claims. Keep feature sets claim-level; join members only when a member attribute is explicitly required, and then confirm the m:1 cardinality, match rate and unmatched-key count from the manifest relationships before trusting joined counts.

When the task text asks for a leakage or guardrail assessment and the catalogue offers a matching component that is off by default (e.g. leakage_assessment), switch it on and pick features so that its flagged_in_plan list is empty; do not rely on prose alone to satisfy an explicit assessment requirement.

For any binary label or flag, report positive and negative counts, prevalence and imbalance ratio with denominators before any comparison or model, and include the class_imbalance caveat; a minority class of a few percent also means per-value cells in high-cardinality categoricals are small, so add the small_groups caveat when breaking the minority class down by category.

In write_report set show_denominators=true and cite_artifacts=true, and match caveats to the task rather than the empty default: synthetic_data and no_operational_use for any fraud or high-cost work, association_not_causation for any group comparison, descriptive_only when no model is fitted, model_limitations only when one is, sample_preview only when a sample is used. Omit caveats that do not apply.

Report both mean and median for dollar amounts, service units and length of stay; these fields are right-skewed, so a mean alone misrepresents typical claims, especially when high-cost claims are the subject.
